newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: IMF S.African aid inevitable by end-Feb - economist.
newsitem.headline: IMF S.African aid inevitable by end-Feb - economist.

text.p: South Africa will have no choice but to seek a loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) by the end of February next year, according to economist Vic de Klerk at stockbroker PLJ van Rensburg.
"We are predicting that it is inevitable that the IMF standby facility will have to be used before the end of February next year," he said in a research note.
"Without it South Africa will be unable to meet its obligations in terms of foreign exchange."
De Klerk said South Africa was likely to see negative cash flow of 7.2 billion rand over the next four months, comprising:
- 2.0 billion for settlement of net sales by foreigners of gilts and shares in October and November;
- 1.9 billion for the purchase by Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd of Dieter Bock's 18 percent stake in Lonrho Plc ;
- 1.0 for the expected current account deficit in November and December;
- 0.8 billion for the expected current account deficit in January and February;
- and 1.5 billion for repayment of a 250 million Ecu loan.
This could be offset by proceeds of 9.0 billion rand from a $2.0 billion IMF standby loan, giving a net positive cash flow of 1.8 billion.
Without such help, South African reserves will fall to unacceptable levels, he said. End-October official reserves stood at just over 10 billion rand, equivalent to four weeks import cover.
Under IMF rules, South Africa would be able to draw up to 100 percent of its IMF quota -- or some $2 billion -- for use as a standby or extended fund facility.
IMF managing director Michel Camdessus said this month that the institution was prepared to support South Africa's reserves and provide funding, if asked.
But many in the ANC are wary of the stigma attached to IMF aid, following unpopular IMF interventions elsewhere in Africa.
